paragraphs: However strongly the vices and prejudices of the Native Americans of North America may stand in the way of their becoming farmers and civilized, necessity sometimes forces them to it. Several of the Southern nations, among them the Cherokees and the Creeks, *n found themselves surrounded by Europeans. These Europeans had landed on the shores of the Atlantic, and, whether they came down the Ohio or up the Mississippi, they reached the tribes’ borders at the same time. These tribes have not been driven from place to place, as their Northern brethren were. Instead, they have been gradually hemmed into narrow limits, like game in a thicket before the hunters plunge into the interior. Placed between civilization and death, they found themselves obliged to live by degrading labor, like the whites. They took up agriculture, and, without entirely giving up their old habits and customs, they sacrificed only as much as was necessary to survive.

n [ These nations are now swallowed up in the States of Georgia, Tennessee, Alabama, and Mississippi. There were formerly four great nations in the South (remnants of which still exist): the Choctaws, the Chickasaws, the Creeks, and the Cherokees. The remnants of these four nations amounted, in 1830, to about 75,000 individuals. It is estimated that about 300,000 Native Americans now remain in the territory occupied or claimed by the Anglo-American Union. (See Proceedings of the Indian Board in the City of New York.) The official documents supplied to Congress put the number at 313,130. A reader who wants to know the names and numerical strength of all the tribes living in Anglo-American territory should consult the documents I refer to. (Legislative Documents, 20th Congress, No. 117, pp. 90-105.) [In the Census of 1870 it is stated that the Indian population of the United States is only 25,731, of whom 7,241 are in California.]]

The Cherokees went further. They created a written language and established a permanent form of government. And since everything moves fast in the New World, they set up a newspaper before they all had clothes. *o
o [ I brought back with me to France one or two copies of this unusual publication.]

The growth of European habits among these Native Americans has been remarkably speeded up by the mixed race that has arisen among them. *p Drawing its education from the father’s side, without entirely losing the savage customs of the mother, the person of mixed race forms the natural link between civilization and barbarism. Wherever this mixed race has multiplied, the savage state has been modified, and a great change has taken place in the customs of the people. *q

p [ See in the Report of the Committee on Indian Affairs, 21st Congress, No. 227, p. 23, the reasons for the increase of people of mixed blood among the Cherokees. The principal cause dates from the War of Independence. Many Anglo-Americans of Georgia, having taken the side of England, were forced to retreat among the Native Americans, where they married.]

q [ Unhappily the mixed race has been less numerous and less influential in North America than in any other country. The American continent was peopled by two great nations of Europe, the French and the English. The French were quick to form ties with the daughters of the natives. But there was an unfortunate affinity between the Native American character and their own. Instead of giving the savages the tastes and habits of civilized life, the French too often became passionately fond of the wild freedom they found them in. They became the most dangerous inhabitants of the wilderness, and won the friendship of the Native Americans by exaggerating both their vices and their virtues. M. de Senonville, the governor of Canada, wrote to Louis XIV in 1685: “It has long been believed that in order to civilize the savages we ought to draw them nearer to us. But there is every reason to suppose we have been mistaken. Those which have been brought into contact with us have not become French, and the French who have lived among them are changed into savages, affecting to dress and live like them.” (“History of New France,” by Charlevoix, vol. ii., p. 345.) The Englishman, by contrast, stayed stubbornly attached to the customs and even the most trivial habits of his forefathers. He has remained in the midst of the American wilderness just what he was in the heart of European cities. He would allow no contact with savages whom he despised, and he carefully avoided any union of his race with theirs. Thus, while the French exercised no wholesome influence over the Native Americans, the English have always remained strangers to them.]

The success of the Cherokees proves that Native Americans are capable of civilization, but it does not prove that they will succeed in it. The difficulty they find in submitting to civilization comes from a general cause, which it is almost impossible for them to escape. A careful look at history shows that, in general, barbarous nations have raised themselves to civilization gradually, and by their own efforts. Whenever they have drawn knowledge from a foreign people, they have stood toward it as conquerors, not as a conquered nation. When the conquered nation is educated and the conquerors are half savage, as when the Northern nations invaded Rome or the Mongols invaded China, the power that victory gives the barbarian is enough to keep up his importance among civilized men and to let him rank as their equal until he becomes their rival. The one has might on his side, the other has intelligence; the former admires the knowledge and the arts of the conquered, and the latter envies the power of the conquerors. The barbarians at length admit civilized man into their palaces, and he in turn opens his schools to the barbarians. But when the side that holds the physical force also holds the intellectual advantage, the conquered party seldom becomes civilized: it retreats, or is destroyed. It may therefore be said, in a general way, that savages go out in arms to seek knowledge, but that they do not accept it when it comes to them.

If the Native American tribes that now live in the heart of the continent could summon up enough energy to try to civilize themselves, they might possibly succeed. Already superior to the barbarous nations around them, they would gradually gain strength and experience. When the Europeans appeared on their borders, they would be in a position, if not to maintain their independence, at least to assert their right to the soil and to merge with the conquerors. But the misfortune of the Native Americans is that they have come into contact with a civilized people that is also (it must be admitted) the most avaricious nation on the globe, while they are still semi-barbarous. They find despots in their teachers, and they receive knowledge from the hand of oppression. Living in the freedom of the woods, the North American Native was poor, but he felt inferior to no one. As soon as he wants to enter the social scale of the whites, however, he takes the lowest rank in society, for he enters the circle of science and wealth ignorant and poor. He has led a life of agitation, beset with evils and dangers but filled at the same time with proud emotions. *r Now he is obliged to submit to a wearisome, obscure, and degraded state, and to earn the bread that feeds him by hard and ignoble labor. In his eyes these are the only results civilization can boast of, and even this much he is not sure to obtain.

r [ The adventurous life of the hunter has a certain irresistible charm, which seizes the heart of man and carries him away in spite of reason and experience. The memoirs of Tanner show this plainly. Tanner is a European who was carried off by Native Americans at the age of six and remained with them in the woods for thirty years. Nothing can be imagined more appalling than the miseries he describes. He tells us of tribes without a chief, families without a nation to call their own, men in a state of isolation, and the wrecks of powerful tribes wandering at random amid the ice and snow and desolate solitudes of Canada. Hunger and cold pursue them, and every day their lives are in danger. Among these men, customs have lost their hold and traditions are without power. They become more and more savage. Tanner shared in all these miseries. He knew he was of European origin. He was not kept away from the whites by force; on the contrary, he came every year to trade with them, entered their homes, and saw their comforts. He knew that whenever he chose to return to civilized life he was perfectly able to do so, and he remained thirty years in the wilderness. When he came into civilized society, he declared that the rough existence he described had a secret charm for him that he could not define. He went back to it again and again. At length he abandoned it with bitter regret, and when he was finally settled among the whites, several of his children refused to share his calm and easy situation. I saw Tanner myself at the lower end of Lake Superior; he seemed to me more like a savage than a civilized man. His book is written without either taste or order, but, even unintentionally, it gives a vivid picture of the prejudices, the passions, the vices, and above all the destitution in which he lived.]

When Native Americans try to imitate their European neighbors and to till the earth as the settlers do, they are immediately exposed to very formidable competition. The white man is skilled in the craft of agriculture; the Native American is a rough beginner in an art he does not know. The white man reaps abundant crops without difficulty, while the Native American meets a thousand obstacles in raising the fruits of the earth.

The European lives among a population whose wants he knows and shares. The savage is isolated in the midst of a hostile people, with whose customs, language, and laws he is imperfectly acquainted, but without whose help he cannot live. He can obtain the means of comfort only by bartering his goods for the goods of the European, since the help of his own countrymen is wholly insufficient to meet his wants. When the Native American wants to sell the produce of his labor, he cannot always find a buyer, while the European readily finds a market. And the former can produce only at considerable cost what the latter sells at a very low price. Thus the Native American has no sooner escaped the evils to which barbarous nations are exposed than he is subjected to the still greater miseries of civilized communities. He finds it scarcely less difficult to live in the midst of our abundance than in the depths of his own wilderness.

He has not yet lost the habits of his wandering life; the traditions of his fathers and his passion for the chase are still alive within him. The wild pleasures that once animated him in the woods painfully excite his troubled imagination, and his former hardships seem less harsh to him, his former dangers less appalling. He contrasts the independence he enjoyed among his equals with the servile position he holds in civilized society. On the other hand, the wilderness that was so long his free home is still close at hand; a few hours’ march will bring him back to it. The whites offer him a sum, which seems considerable to him, for the ground he has begun to clear. This money from the Europeans may possibly give him the means of a happy and peaceful living in remoter regions. So he leaves the plow, takes up his native weapons again, and returns to the wilderness forever. *s The condition of the Creeks and Cherokees, to which I have already alluded, fully confirms the truth of this sad picture.

s [ The destructive influence of highly civilized nations on those less civilized has been shown by the Europeans themselves. About a century ago the French founded the town of Vincennes on the Wabash, in the middle of the wilderness, and they lived there in great plenty until the arrival of the American settlers. The Americans first ruined the earlier inhabitants by their competition and afterward bought their lands at a very low price. When M. de Volney, from whom I borrow these details, passed through Vincennes, the number of the French was reduced to a hundred individuals, most of whom were about to move to Louisiana or to Canada. These French settlers were worthy people, but idle and uneducated; they had picked up many of the habits of savages. The Americans, who were perhaps their inferiors from a moral point of view, were immeasurably superior to them in intelligence: they were industrious, well informed, rich, and used to governing their own community.

I myself saw in Canada, where the intellectual difference between the two races is less striking, that the English are the masters of commerce and manufacturing in the Canadian country. They spread on all sides and confine the French within limits that scarcely suffice to hold them. In the same way, in Louisiana, almost all activity in commerce and manufacturing is concentrated in the hands of the Anglo-Americans.

But the case of Texas is still more striking. The State of Texas is a part of Mexico and lies on the frontier between that country and the United States. In the last few years the Anglo-Americans have moved into this province, which is still thinly peopled. They buy land, they produce the commodities of the country, and they replace the original population. It is easy to foresee that if Mexico takes no steps to check this change, the province of Texas will very shortly cease to belong to that government.

If the different degrees of European civilization, which differ comparatively little, produce results of such magnitude, we can readily imagine the consequences that must follow when the most advanced European civilization collides with Native American savages.]

In the little they have done, the Native Americans have unquestionably shown as much natural genius as the peoples of Europe in their most important undertakings. But nations, like individuals, need time to learn, whatever their intelligence and zeal. While the savages were engaged in the work of civilization, the Europeans kept surrounding them on every side and confining them within narrower limits. The two races gradually met, and they now stand in immediate juxtaposition. The Native American is already superior to his barbarous parent, but he is still very far below his white neighbor. With their resources and acquired knowledge, the Europeans soon took for themselves most of the advantages the natives might have drawn from owning the soil. They have settled in the country; they have bought land at a very low price or occupied it by force; and the Native Americans have been ruined by a competition they had no means of resisting. They were isolated in their own country, and their race was only a colony of troublesome aliens in the midst of a numerous and domineering people. *t

t [ See in the Legislative Documents (21st Congress, No. 89) instances of every kind of excess committed by the whites on the territory of the Native Americans. The whites took possession of part of their lands until the troops of Congress forced them to withdraw, or they carried off their cattle, burned their houses, cut down their corn, and did violence to their persons. It appears nevertheless from all these documents that the claims of the natives are constantly protected by the government against the abuse of force. The Union has a representative agent continually employed to reside among the Native Americans, and the report of the Cherokee agent, which is among the documents I have referred to, is almost always favorable to them. “The intrusion of whites,” he says, “upon the lands of the Cherokees would cause ruin to the poor, helpless, and inoffensive inhabitants.” And he further remarks, about the attempt of the State of Georgia to establish a division line limiting the boundaries of the Cherokees, that the line drawn, having been made by the whites and entirely upon ex parte evidence of their several rights, was of no validity whatever.]

Washington said in one of his messages to Congress, “We are more enlightened and more powerful than the Indian nations, we are therefore bound in honor to treat them with kindness and even with generosity.” But this virtuous and high-minded policy has not been followed. The greed of the settlers is usually backed by the tyranny of the government. The Cherokees and the Creeks are established on the territory they inhabited before the Europeans settled, and the Americans have often treated with them as with foreign nations. Even so, the surrounding States have not agreed to recognize them as independent peoples, and attempts have been made to subject these children of the woods to Anglo-American magistrates, laws, and customs. *u Destitution had driven these unfortunate people to civilization, and oppression now drives them back to their former condition. Many of them abandon the soil they had begun to clear and return to their savage way of life.
u [ In 1829 the State of Alabama divided the Creek territory into counties and subjected the Native American population to the power of European magistrates.

In 1830 the State of Mississippi assimilated the Choctaws and Chickasaws to the white population, and declared that any of them who took the title of chief would be punished by a fine of $1,000 and a year’s imprisonment. When these laws were enforced upon the Choctaws, who lived in that district, the tribe assembled. Their chief told them what the whites intended and read them some of the laws they were meant to submit to. They unanimously declared that it was better to retreat into the wilds again at once.]
Chapter XVIII: Future Condition of Three Races — Part III

If we consider the tyrannical measures adopted by the legislatures of the Southern States, the conduct of their Governors, and the decrees of their courts of justice, we shall be convinced that the final aim of their policy is the complete expulsion of the Native Americans. The Americans of that part of the Union look on the aborigines with jealousy. *v They know that these tribes have not yet lost the traditions of savage life, and before civilization has fixed them permanently to the soil, they intend to force them to withdraw by driving them to despair. The Creeks and Cherokees, oppressed by the several States, have appealed to the central government. It is by no means indifferent to their misfortunes and sincerely wants to save the remnant of the natives and keep them in free possession of the territory that the Union is pledged to respect. *w But the several States offer such formidable resistance to carrying out this plan that the government is obliged to consent to the extermination of a few barbarous tribes, so as not to endanger the safety of the American Union.

v [ The Georgians, who are so much troubled by the nearness of the Native Americans, live in a territory that does not at present hold more than seven inhabitants to the square mile. In France there are one hundred and sixty-two inhabitants to the same extent of country.]

w [ In 1818 Congress appointed commissioners to visit the Arkansas Territory, accompanied by a deputation of Creeks, Choctaws, and Chickasaws. This expedition was commanded by Messrs. Kennerly, M’Coy, Wash Hood, and John Bell. See the different reports of the commissioners, and their journal, in the Documents of Congress, No. 87, House of Representatives.]

But the federal government, which cannot protect the Native Americans, would gladly ease the hardships of their lot. With this intention, proposals have been made to transport them at public expense to more remote regions.

Between the thirty-third and thirty-seventh degrees of north latitude lies a vast tract of country, which has taken the name of Arkansas from the principal river that waters it. It is bounded on one side by the borders of Mexico and on the other by the Mississippi. Numberless streams cross it in every direction; the climate is mild and the soil productive, but only a few wandering hordes of savages live there. The government of the Union wants to transport the broken remnants of the indigenous population of the South to the part of this country nearest Mexico and at a great distance from the American settlements.

We were assured, toward the end of the year 1831, that 10,000 Native Americans had already gone down to the shores of the Arkansas, and fresh detachments were constantly following them. But Congress has been unable to arouse a unanimous determination in those it wants to protect. Some, indeed, are willing to leave the seat of oppression, but the most educated members of the community refuse to abandon their new homes and their growing crops. They believe that the work of civilization, once interrupted, will never be resumed. They fear that the domestic habits they have so recently acquired may be irretrievably lost in a country that is still barbarous, where nothing is prepared for the support of an agricultural people. They know that hostile hordes will oppose their entry into those wilds, and that they have lost the energy of barbarians without gaining the resources of civilization to resist their attacks. Moreover, they readily see that the settlement proposed to them is merely a temporary expedient. Who can assure them that they will at length be allowed to live in peace in their new retreat? The United States pledges itself to keep its obligation, but the territory they now occupy was formerly secured to them by the most solemn oaths of Anglo-American good faith. *x The American government does not indeed rob them of their lands, but it allows constant incursions upon them. In a few years the same white population that now crowds around them will track them to the solitudes of the Arkansas. They will then be exposed to the same evils without the same remedies, and since the limits of the earth will at last fail them, their only refuge is the grave.

x [ The fifth article of the treaty made with the Creeks in August, 1790, is in the following words: — “The United States solemnly guarantee to the Creek nation all their land within the limits of the United States.”

The seventh article of the treaty concluded in 1791 with the Cherokees says: — “The United States solemnly guarantee to the Cherokee nation all their lands not hereby ceded.” The following article declared that if any citizen of the United States or other settler not of the Indian race should establish himself on the territory of the Cherokees, the United States would withdraw their protection from that individual and hand him over to be punished as the Cherokee nation should think fit.]

The Union treats the Native Americans with less greed and harshness than the policy of the several States does, but the two governments are equally lacking in good faith. The States extend to the tribes what they are pleased to call the benefits of their laws, believing that the tribes will withdraw rather than submit. And the central government, which promises these unhappy people a permanent refuge, is well aware that it cannot secure it to them. *y

y [ This does not prevent them from promising to do so in the most solemn manner. See the letter of the President addressed to the Creek Indians, March 23, 1829 (Proceedings of the Indian Board, in the city of New York, p. 5): “Beyond the great river Mississippi, where a part of your nation has gone, your father has provided a country large enough for all of you, and he advises you to remove to it. There your white brothers will not trouble you; they will have no claim to the land, and you can live upon it, you and all your children, as long as the grass grows, or the water runs, in peace and plenty. It will be yours forever.”

The Secretary of War, in a letter written to the Cherokees on April 18, 1829 (see the same work, p. 6), tells them that they cannot expect to keep possession of the lands they then occupied. But he gives them the most positive assurance of uninterrupted peace if they will move beyond the Mississippi. It is as if the power that could not protect them then would be able to protect them later!]

Thus the tyranny of the States forces the savages to retire, and the Union, by its promises and resources, makes their retreat easier. These measures tend to precisely the same end. *z “By the will of our Father in Heaven, the Governor of the whole world,” said the Cherokees in their petition to Congress, *a “the red man of America has become small, and the white man great and renowned. When the ancestors of the people of these United States first came to the shores of America they found the red man strong: though he was ignorant and savage, yet he received them kindly, and gave them dry land to rest their weary feet. They met in peace, and shook hands in token of friendship. Whatever the white man wanted and asked of the Indian, the latter willingly gave. At that time the Indian was the lord, and the white man the suppliant. But now the scene has changed. The strength of the red man has become weakness. As his neighbors increased in numbers his power became less and less, and now, of the many and powerful tribes who once covered these United States, only a few are to be seen—a few whom a sweeping pestilence has left. The northern tribes, who were once so numerous and powerful, are now nearly extinct. Thus it has happened to the red man of America. Shall we, who are remnants, share the same fate?”

z [ To form a correct idea of the policy followed by the several States and the Union toward the Native Americans, one must consult, first, “The Laws of the Colonial and State Governments relating to the Indian Inhabitants.” (See the Legislative Documents, 21st Congress, No. 319.) Second, the Laws of the Union on the same subject, and especially that of March 30, 1802. (See Story’s “Laws of the United States.”) Third, the Report of Mr. Cass, Secretary of War, relative to Indian Affairs, November 29, 1823.]
a [ December 18, 1829.]

“The land on which we stand we have received as an inheritance from our fathers, who possessed it from time immemorial, as a gift from our common Father in Heaven. They bequeathed it to us as their children, and we have sacredly kept it, as containing the remains of our beloved men. This right of inheritance we have never ceded nor ever forfeited. Permit us to ask what better right can the people have to a country than the right of inheritance and immemorial peaceable possession? We know it is said of late by the State of Georgia and by the Executive of the United States, that we have forfeited this right; but we think this is said gratuitously. At what time have we made the forfeit? What great crime have we committed, whereby we must forever be divested of our country and rights? Was it when we were hostile to the United States, and took part with the King of Great Britain, during the struggle for independence? If so, why was not this forfeiture declared in the first treaty of peace between the United States and our beloved men? Why was not such an article as the following inserted in the treaty:—‘The United States give peace to the Cherokees, but, for the part they took in the late war, declare them to be but tenants at will, to be removed when the convenience of the States, within whose chartered limits they live, shall require it’? That was the proper time to assume such a possession. But it was not thought of, nor would our forefathers have agreed to any treaty whose tendency was to deprive them of their rights and their country.”

Such is the language of the Native Americans. Their assertions are true and their forebodings unavoidable. From whichever side we consider the destiny of the aborigines of North America, their calamities appear beyond remedy. If they remain barbarous, they are forced to retire. If they try to civilize their customs, contact with a more civilized community subjects them to oppression and destitution. They perish if they keep wandering from waste to waste, and if they try to settle, they must still perish. The help of Europeans is necessary to teach them, but the approach of Europeans corrupts them and drives them back into savage life. They refuse to change their habits as long as their wilderness is their own, and it is too late to change them when they are forced to submit.

The Spaniards hunted the Native Americans with bloodhounds, like wild beasts. They sacked the New World with no more restraint or compassion than a city taken by storm. But destruction must cease and frenzy must end. The remnant of the Native American population that had escaped the massacre mixed with its conquerors and in the end adopted their religion and their customs. *b The conduct of the Americans of the United States toward the aborigines, on the other hand, is marked by a singular attachment to the formalities of law. As long as the Native Americans remain in their barbarous condition, the Americans take no part in their affairs. They treat them as independent nations, and they do not take possession of their hunting grounds without a treaty of purchase. And if a Native American nation happens to be so encroached upon that it cannot live on its territory, they give it brotherly help in transporting it to a grave far enough away from the land of its fathers.

b [ The honor of this result, however, is by no means due to the Spaniards. If the Native American tribes had not been tillers of the ground when the Europeans arrived, they would unquestionably have been destroyed in South America as well as in North America.]

The Spaniards could not exterminate the Native American race by those unparalleled atrocities that brand them with indelible shame, nor did they even succeed in wholly depriving it of its rights. But the Americans of the United States have accomplished both purposes with singular ease: quietly, legally, philanthropically, without shedding blood, and without violating a single great principle of morality in the eyes of the world. *c It is impossible to destroy men with more respect for the laws of humanity.

c [ See, among other documents, the report made by Mr. Bell in the name of the Committee on Indian Affairs, February 24, 1830, in which it is most logically established and most learnedly proved that “the fundamental principle that the Indians had no right by virtue of their ancient possession either of will or sovereignty, has never been abandoned either expressly or by implication.” Reading this report, which was evidently drawn up by an experienced hand, one is astonished at how easily the author disposes of all arguments founded on reason and natural right, which he labels abstract and theoretical principles. The more I consider the difference between civilized and uncivilized man with regard to the principles of justice, the more I observe that the former disputes the justice of those rights that the latter simply violates.]

[I leave this chapter wholly unchanged, for it has always seemed to me one of the most eloquent and touching parts of this book. But it has ceased to be prophetic; the destruction of the Native American race in the United States is already complete. In 1870 only 25,731 Native Americans remained in the whole territory of the Union, and by far the largest part of them live in California, Michigan, Wisconsin, Dakota, and New Mexico and Nevada. In New England, Pennsylvania, and New York the race is extinct, and the predictions of M. de Tocqueville are fulfilled. — Translator’s Note.]
Situation of the Black Population in the United States, and Dangers with Which Its Presence Threatens the Whites

Why it is more difficult to abolish slavery, and to efface all traces of it, among the moderns than it was among the ancients — In the United States the prejudices of whites against Black people seem to increase in proportion as slavery is abolished — Situation of Black people in the Northern and Southern States — Why the Americans abolish slavery — Servitude, which debases the slave, impoverishes the master — Contrast between the left and the right bank of the Ohio — To what this is attributable — The Black race, as well as slavery, recedes toward the South — Explanation of this fact — Difficulties attendant upon the abolition of slavery in the South — Dangers to come — General anxiety — Foundation of a Black colony in Africa — Why the Americans of the South increase the hardships of slavery, while they are distressed at its continuance.

The Native Americans will perish in the same isolation in which they have lived. But the destiny of Black people is to some extent interwoven with that of the Europeans. These two races are attached to each other without intermingling, and they are equally unable either to separate entirely or to combine. The most formidable of all the ills that threaten the future existence of the Union comes from the presence of a Black population on its territory. When the observer looks for the cause of the present embarrassments or the future dangers of the United States, he is invariably led to this as a primary fact.

The lasting evils that afflict mankind are usually produced by the violent or growing efforts of men. But there is one calamity that crept stealthily into the world and was at first scarcely distinguishable amid the ordinary abuses of power. It began with an individual whose name history has not preserved. It was carried like some accursed seed to one portion of the soil, but afterward it fed itself, grew without effort, and spreads naturally with the society to which it belongs. I need hardly add that this calamity is slavery. Christianity suppressed slavery, but the Christians of the sixteenth century reestablished it, as an exception, indeed, to their social system, and restricted to one of the races of mankind. Yet the wound thus inflicted on humanity, though less extensive, was at the same time made far harder to cure.

It is important to distinguish accurately between slavery itself and its consequences. The immediate evils produced by slavery were very nearly the same in antiquity as they are among the moderns, but the consequences of these evils were different. Among the ancients, the slave belonged to the same race as his master and was often the superior of the two in education *d and learning. Freedom was the only distinction between them, and when freedom was granted they were easily blended together. The ancients, then, had a very simple means of avoiding slavery and its evil consequences, which was emancipation; and they succeeded as soon as they adopted this measure generally. This is not to say that in ancient States no traces of servitude lingered for some time after servitude itself was abolished. There is a natural prejudice that leads men to despise anyone who was once their inferior long after he has become their equal. The real inequality produced by fortune or by law is always followed by an imaginary inequality planted in the customs of the people. Nevertheless, among the ancients this secondary consequence of slavery lasted only a limited time, for the freedman so completely resembled those born free that it soon became impossible to tell him apart from them.

d [ It is well known that several of the most distinguished authors of antiquity, among them Aesop and Terence, were, or had been, slaves. Slaves were not always taken from barbarous nations, and the chances of war reduced highly civilized men to servitude.]

The greatest difficulty in antiquity was changing the law; among the moderns it is changing the customs. And as far as we are concerned, the real obstacles begin where those of the ancients ended. This comes from the fact that, among the moderns, the abstract and transient fact of slavery is fatally joined to the physical and permanent fact of color. The tradition of slavery dishonors the race, and the distinctiveness of the race keeps the tradition of slavery alive. No African has ever voluntarily emigrated to the shores of the New World, and from this it must be inferred that all the Black people now found in that hemisphere are either slaves or freedmen. Thus the Black person passes the lasting mark of his disgrace on to all his descendants, and although the law may abolish slavery, God alone can erase the traces of its existence.
